title: Luke 22:24–38
context: At the table, Jesus corrects rivalry through his own service, promises kingdom fellowship, and warns Peter of satanic testing and denial while assuring him of intercession and return. Both traditions call disciples away from self-confidence toward grace-dependent obedience; they differ over how Peter’s preservation informs the doctrine of perseverance. The difficult sword language must be read beside the coming arrest, Jesus’ healing, and his rejection of armed rescue rather than turned into permission for coercive mission.

verses.text: A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
verses.arminianNotes: A dispute over greatness interrupts the solemn setting of the meal. Arminian readers recognize that disciples still need grace to resist rivalry and respond to correction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see remaining sin among Christ’s followers. Their failures expose the need for sanctification rather than justifying rivalry as harmless because they are disciples.

verses.text: He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus contrasts kingdom leadership with domination disguised by honorable titles. Arminian readers see a challenge to seek others’ good rather than prestige under religious cover.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise reject the use of authority for self-exaltation. Public recognition as generous or important does not itself demonstrate the servant character Christ requires.

verses.text: But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus commands the greater disciple to take the lower place and serve. Arminian readers see grace-enabled humility as a concrete responsibility, not merely an inward sentiment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise understand service as the fruit of following Christ. Authority in his community should be exercised for others’ benefit rather than personal advancement.

verses.text: For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus himself supplies the pattern of service at the table. Arminian readers ground the call to humility in his loving action rather than in earning his acceptance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Lord’s service overturning status competition. Christ’s example forms grateful obedience without reducing his saving mission to moral example alone.

verses.text: “But you are those who have continued with me in my trials.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus acknowledges companions who have remained with him in trials. Arminian readers see continuing loyalty valued without denying the severe failure about to be predicted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize grace at work in imperfect disciples. Christ’s commendation does not imply sinless constancy or eliminate their continuing need for his intercession.

verses.text: I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me,
verses.arminianNotes: The kingdom is conferred as a gift patterned on the Father’s gift to Jesus. Arminian readers see gracious participation, not a reward detached from relationship with Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the initiative of the Father and Son. The disciples receive their place in the kingdom rather than constructing it through status seeking.

verses.text: that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Table fellowship and governing responsibility replace their immediate rivalry with a larger promise. Arminian readers locate this honor in Christ’s gift rather than personal superiority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize promised participation in Christ’s reign. Interpretations of the twelve tribes and future judging vary and should not be assigned automatically to either soteriological tradition.

verses.text: The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat,
verses.arminianNotes: Satan seeks to sift the disciples, making spiritual danger real rather than imaginary. Arminian readers emphasize dependence on grace and vigilance, not confidence in personal resolve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take satanic assault seriously while recognizing its limits under God. The plural address concerns the disciples together before Jesus singles out Peter for prayer.

verses.text: but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ prayer supports Peter through failure toward return and service. Arminian readers see powerful preserving grace that calls for a real repentant response, not denial that believers face danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s effective intercession preserving Peter’s faith through grievous sin. His promised return illustrates restoration secured by grace rather than immunity from serious falls.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm Christ’s intercession and Peter’s real return after grievous failure. Arminian readers emphasize preserving grace and the necessity of repentant response without generalizing Peter’s case into unconditional perseverance for all believers; Reformed readers see his restoration as an illustration of Christ’s effective preservation of his people.

verses.text: He said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!”
verses.arminianNotes: Peter promises prison and death but misunderstands his own weakness. Arminian readers see a warning that sincere resolve cannot replace prayerful dependence on divine help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish confident professions from sustaining grace. Peter’s courage will fail, exposing how little assurance can safely rest on an estimate of one’s own strength.

verses.text: He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will by no means crow today until you deny that you know me three times.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus predicts Peter’s three denials with precision. Arminian readers affirm Christ’s foreknowledge without making Peter’s sinful speech involuntary or therefore innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm Christ’s knowledge and Peter’s responsibility. The prediction prepares for restoration without minimizing the seriousness of a disciple denying his Lord.

verses.text: He said to them, “When I sent you out without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.”
verses.arminianNotes: The disciples acknowledge that Jesus provided during their earlier mission. Arminian readers see remembered grace strengthening trust as circumstances change, not a guarantee that hardship will disappear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize faithful provision through a particular commission. The memory supports dependence while the next instruction shows that practical arrangements can legitimately change.

verses.text: Then he said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag. Whoever has none, let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus prepares the disciples for a harsher setting using language of supplies and a sword. Arminian readers should read this beside his rebuke of violent action, not as permission for coercive mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise interpret this difficult command within the arrest narrative and its fulfillment theme. Practical readiness must not become a warrant to spread the kingdom by violence.

verses.text: For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘He was counted with transgressors.’ For that which concerns me is being fulfilled.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus explains the coming crisis through Scripture’s picture of being counted with transgressors. Arminian readers see voluntary redemptive obedience rather than guilt of his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize the innocent Savior entering the place of the condemned in fulfillment of Scripture. The verse explains his mission, not an endorsement of the disciples becoming violent offenders.

verses.text: They said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” He said to them, “That is enough.”
verses.arminianNotes: The disciples point to two swords, and Jesus ends the exchange. Arminian readers recognize interpretive uncertainty rather than treating the reply as an unqualified military authorization.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the reply alongside Jesus’ later healing and refusal of armed rescue. Neither tradition should make this brief exchange a license for religious violence.
